canberra.title: Canberra mother’s fury after anaphylactic daughter dropped from specialist waitlist
canberra.snippet: A Canberra mother has expressed her fear that children could die from preventable allergic reactions after the public health system kicke...
canberra.content:
Canberra Health Services’ outpatient specialist referral waitlist had more than 65,000 people on the books. Photo: James Coleman.

A Canberra mother has expressed her fear that children could die from preventable allergic reactions after the public health system kicked her daughter off the outpatient specialist appointments waitlist.

ANU academic Dr Liz Allen was shocked when a Canberra Health Services letter arrived in the mail, addressed to her nine-year-old daughter.

They’d been referred to the public paediatric allergy clinic in January 2024 after her daughter suffered several anaphylactic reactions – some leading to stays in Canberra Hospital’s emergency department.

The letter stated that Dr Allen’s daughter’s referral no longer “[met] the criteria for a specialist appointment with CHS” and that her referral had been closed.

“I’m gobsmacked this is how we would treat people in need … [families such as ours] are already under stressful circumstances as we have kids with higher health needs. To be treated like this – I’ve got no words,” she said.

“Our GP has since retired, so we’re now going to have to get all referral materials – including discharge materials from the emergency department – again.”

Dr Liz Allen was shocked to receive a letter stating her anaphylactic daughter no longer met the criteria for an outpatient specialist appointment at Canberra’s paediatric allergy clinic. Photo: Instagram.

On 8 October, CHS posted a statement on its website that it was reviewing all outpatient services so people “with the greatest clinical need” could access specialist care sooner.

There are about 65,000 people waiting for an outpatient appointment.

The paediatric allergy clinic’s waiting time is longer than six years.

Dr Allen questioned how children having anaphylactic reactions didn’t meet the criteria for “greatest need”.

“Essentially, what this letter says … [is] your kid, who could die from an allergic response, doesn’t meet the criteria to see a specialist and receive life-saving treatment,” she said.

“If kids with anaphylactic reactions don’t meet the criteria for an allergy outpatient service, what does?”

CHS outlined on its website that the criteria had been updated as suggested by the independent Walsh Report into the ACT’s health system.

Dr Allen said this letter was the only communication she’d received, apart from a confirmation phone call, since her referral was submitted in 2024.

She questioned how a decision could be made to remove people from wait lists without contacting patients to find out if their circumstances had changed.

“There’s no excuse for this, other than a willful act to very opaquely review systems without contacting affected people, and then change criteria without any [public] consultation,” Dr Allen said.

“This cannot be the way that a health service that operates in the most affluent Territory in the country … is treating its citizens.

“The risk is there could be children who die from preventable, preventable reactions.”

Dr Allen posted her daughter’s letter on social media.

Dozens of people responded, recounting their own experiences.

One commenter stated they’d been told at their son’s last appointment that he couldn’t be seen again for another four years.

“We were told … there’s no funding for the [sic] paediatric anymore,” they stated.

Another person who received such a letter for their daughter had been on the waitlist since 2018. One parent’s child aged out of the system while waiting for an appointment.

And from a professional: “6 years !!?? I am actually shook as a paediatric nurse.”

Dr Liz Allen took to Instagram to express her shock and outrage that her daughter had been removed from a specialist waitlist. Photo: Instagram.

Dr Allen said she’d also been contacted privately, including by a practising private paediatric allergenist who offered their services to CHS, but was told CHS didn’t have the money to pay for their time.

“The [people] and goodwill is there,” she said.

“So it looks like [CHS] can’t afford to pay for vital services – is that where we’re at? That’s life-threatening.”

Several said they’d resorted to going to a specialist hub in Goulburn, or even further to Sydney, for treatment.

Private allergy services are available in Canberra, but they can cost hundreds of dollars.

“There will be some people who simply cannot pay to go private,” Dr Allen said.

Opposition Leader and Shadow Health Minister Mark Parton described the situation as “shameful”.

“It exposes the chaos in our health system and raises serious questions about the advice given to the [Health] Minister,” he said.

Mr Parton will move a motion in the Legislative Assembly on Tuesday (27 October) calling on the ACT Government to honour the original waiting lists.

“We understand that they’re going through a process of review, but we don’t believe that that process of review should mean weeding out everyone on the waiting list and starting from scratch,” he said.

“I think we’ve seen over a number of portfolio areas that this government is not a fan of bad report cards, and they will do anything to change those report cards, and one of the ways to get yourself out of a sticky situation of having 65,000 people on waiting lists is to just crash those waiting lists.

“We don’t believe that’s acceptable.”

Independent Kurrajong MLA Thomas Emerson will also move an order for the production of documents (co-sponsored with ACT Greens MLA Rebecca Vassarotti and Mr Parton) for the government to table a number of 2026 papers relating to the Paediatric Allergy Clinic waitlist, complaints about the changed criteria, risk assessments undertaken before the change was enacted, and data relating to how the waitlist has changed in the past five years.

The ACT Government did not respond to questions in time for publication.

canberra.title: Rapist ‘monster’ who held woman captive for two days ‘deserves no mercy’, court told
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence. The violent rapist who inflicted an unimaginable ordeal on his young victim pose...
canberra.content:
Sisituutuumata Fulivai, 47, has faced the ACT Supreme Court for his sentencing hearing. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence.

The violent rapist who inflicted an unimaginable ordeal on his young victim poses a significant risk to women, a court heard when she and her family faced him in court.

Sisituutuumata Fulivai held a young woman captive at his home in Lyneham for two days in June 2024 while raping and repeatedly assaulting her. She eventually managed to fight her way out of his home and fled, naked, onto the street, where she was found by police.

“It was an eternity of a terrifying nightmare,” the woman, aged in her mid-20s, said this week.

“You didn’t just violate my body. You took a machete to my mind and my very sense of safety in this world.

“No person should ever have the chance to meet the monster I did. He is a danger to women and to society.”

The now-47-year-old Tongan man, whom the woman called ‘Matt’, was found guilty of 20 charges at the end of his ACT Supreme Court jury trial.

Her family had travelled for hours to support her when he was originally scheduled to face his sentencing hearing in June.

However, when they arrived, they learned Fulivai had fired his previous solicitors, so the sentencing could not go ahead and was instead adjourned to Monday (26 October).

The woman, who was visibly emotional, told the court she had fought desperately to survive over those days and was now living with crippling post-traumatic stress disorder.

“But the devastation of your actions didn’t stop once I escaped. Your violence bled out, infecting everyone who loves me,” she told him.

But the woman also told him the scars he left were the marks of her survival.

“I have reclaimed my life, my mind and my voice that you tried to erase in an attempt to destroy my identity,” she said.

“I’m far more resilient than you could ever comprehend.”

Fulivai watched on while she spoke. He tried to interrupt the woman’s mother when she started speaking to the court; however, Justice Belinda Baker told him to be quiet.

The mother said Fulivai’s actions had a profound and catastrophic impact on her daughter and their family.

“My vibrant girl is replaced with a shell of her former self,” the mother said.

“He chose to be inhuman … He was planning to kill my child.

“He showed my daughter no mercy; he deserves the same.”

Prosecutor Nathan Deakes said Fulivai’s abuse called for a significant term of imprisonment.

“Your Honour would find it was a protracted, extreme and degrading ordeal,” he said.

“It is the prosecution’s submission that the risk that this offender poses to women is significant.

“Any sentence must recognise the importance of protecting women from sexual violence.”

Mr Deakes noted Fulivai had received multiple sanctions for violence against other inmates during the two years he had spent in custody so far.

His barrister, Christina Muthurajah, said her client would eventually be released from custody and his rehabilitation should still be considered upon sentencing.

She said her client had been a contributing member of the community until a few years ago.

His life took “a sharp turn” in 2023 after he lost his job and his home. Until January 2024, he only had a minor incident on his criminal record.

Justice Baker reserved her decision and will sentence Fulivai, who remains in custody, at a future date.

He was found guilty of 12 counts of assault, three counts of choking, three counts of making a threat to kill, as well as single counts of sexual intercourse without consent and unlawful confinement.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Government contractor suspended after allegedly using job to stalk woman
canberra.snippet: While a man accused of committing a terrifying stalking campaign against a woman he barely knew has been granted bail, he won’t be ...
canberra.content:
Suyash Sinha, 31, leaves court holding his shoes after the court granted him bail. Photo: Albert McKnight.

While a man accused of committing a terrifying stalking campaign against a woman he barely knew has been granted bail, he won’t be returning to his contracting job at the ACT Government after being suspended due to his charge.

Suyash Sinha, a 31-year-old from Franklin, was charged with stalking and was originally refused bail when he first faced the ACT Magistrates Court earlier this month.

The court heard he found a woman on a dating app in January 2026, but when he asked her to start a relationship, she refused.

Despite this, she allegedly continued to receive messages from him during the year. Then, in August 2026, she was shopping at a Coles in Canberra when he allegedly messaged her, described what she was wearing, and said he was at the supermarket too. He had a second job at the supermarket.

The court further heard that as Mr Sinha kept messaging her, the woman became frustrated and agreed to meet him in person to tell him to stop.

When they met at a pub, he allegedly said he worked in finance for the ACT Government and told her the name of one of her siblings, which she had never mentioned to him before.

“Anyone could be looked up in government systems,” he allegedly said.

The woman was afraid and left.

In addition to allegedly continuing to message her, he reportedly also sent her multiple friend requests from different accounts on social media apps during September.

The court heard these accounts allegedly had names like “willbeseeingyousoonnoworry”, “riskingitallforyousexy [her name]”, “Ihateyousomuchgoodbye”, and “sexy [her name] forpresident”.

Mr Sinha spent about two weeks in custody before applying for bail for the second time on Monday (26 October), which the prosecution again opposed.

His lawyer, Satomi Hamon of CODA Criminal Law, said her client had a Masters in Finance and Accounting from the Australian National University and had been tutoring at the university as well as contracting at the ACT Government.

However, the court heard he was suspended without pay from his government job after his employer learned of his charge through media reporting.

Ms Hamon said her client had made various admissions when he was interviewed by police. But she pointed out the stalking allegations ended about a month before he was arrested.

The lawyer said her client had no prior criminal history and argued nothing suggested he couldn’t comply with bail conditions.

The prosecutor, when opposing bail, alleged the messages Mr Sinha sent the woman “effectively describe a person who is unable to take no for an answer”.

She also said police were still investigating his alleged use of government work systems.

Magistrate Ian Temby said the bail application was tricky. He said on one hand, the alleged messages exhibited a degree of “obsessiveness” and meant there was a risk of him endangering the woman’s safety.

But he also agreed with Ms Hamon that nothing suggested he couldn’t comply with bail conditions.

Magistrate Temby granted bail on several conditions, including that Mr Sinha not contact the woman or her family, not use social media, and not access any individual’s personal information in government systems unless required to do so for his job.

The matter was adjourned to 4 November. No plea was entered.

canberra.title: Will Murray: Wagga cult hero to worldwide fame after flood rescue
canberra.snippet: ABC reporter Will Murray has become a worldwide household name after putting down his camera and plunging into floodwaters near Brisbane ...
canberra.content:
26 October 2026

Join the conversation

1

Will Murray also got in the water when working in Wagga. Photo: Will Murray/Facebook.

ABC reporter Will Murray has become a worldwide household name after putting down his camera and plunging into floodwaters near Brisbane to rescue a man from drowning.

The dramatic rescue last Thursday (22 October) has made headlines around the world, with the BBC and New York Times among the international media outlets chasing the story.

But long before his newfound fame, Mr Murray had a cult following in Wagga, where he cut his teeth as a television journalist between 2017 and 2021.

Such was his popularity that a Facebook page called Fans of Will Murray was dedicated to his Riverina reporting, including his penchant for getting stuck into a story – sometimes literally.

Mr Murray was never shy about getting his feet wet, famously wading into the Murrumbidgee River in a shirt and tie while covering the cancellation of the annual Gumi Race.

Region caught up with the 33-year-old to talk about his split-second decision to jump into the water, his newfound international fame and his memories of Wagga and his cult following.

How does it feel to read about yourself in the BBC and New York Times?

Unbelievable and so weird. The BBC one was OK, I was measured. But by the time the New York Times called, it had been such an overwhelming day and I wasn’t proud of that interview.

But I guess it’s always better than being in the news for something negative.

Is Wagga where you really plied your trade as a journalist?

Wagga was my first proper TV gig. I worked in Canberra for a bit doing news updates and Seven Regional sent me to Wagga. I moved to Channel Nine a year later.

We only left Wagga because the local Channel Nine went belly up. My wife Liz, who also worked in media and I were made redundant and moved to Tasmania.

We loved Wagga and didn’t want to leave. I’ve never been involved in better footy clubs or a better community.

It was a massive news market. We covered everything from Culcairn to Young to Griffith. It’s an awesome place.

Will won a best on ground medal after a grand final win in the Riverina League in 2020. Photo: Will Murray Facebook.

You developed a cult following in Wagga and even had a Facebook page dedicated to you – how did that happen?

I was doing a lot of silly things on camera, so a friend of mine made a compilation and put it on a Facebook page dedicated to me.

Thankfully, it is now defunct.

Did you hesitate at all before jumping into the water to rescue the man?

It sounds cliched, but it felt like he was in a really bad spot and about to drown. At that point, everything goes out of your mind.

I thought, who cares about anything else? I could never watch someone drown.

Did you feel your life was in danger, too?

No, this wasn’t the Murrumbidgee. It wasn’t flowing heavily. I thought I could hold on to the fence if needed, but later realised it was barbed wire, so that wouldn’t have been a good idea.

How was the weekend after becoming a worldwide hero?

After the adrenaline crashed on Saturday, I felt really flat. The publicity was crazy. It was too much, but I’m better now.

How do you think your heroics will impact your career?

I think it will wear off really quickly. People have already forgotten.

Did you get time off afterwards?

I did get Friday afternoon off, but I’m back to work today (Monday).

Everyone in Wagga says you’re the ultimate nice guy and always so nice. Surely you’ve done something bad in your life. Tell us.

Just ask my wife, Liz.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: No time to waste as work kicks off on state-of-the-art recycling hub at Hume
canberra.snippet: The ACT is on track to save about $10 million a year, and maybe even make some money, as work officially kicks off on the Territory&#8217...
canberra.content:
Manteena CEO Mark Bauer, Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne and Veolia CEO Craig Barker turning the sod for construction of the new Hume Materials Recovery Facility (MRF). Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT is on track to save about $10 million a year, and maybe even make some money, as work officially kicks off on the Territory’s new Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) at Hume.

It’s been almost four years since the original facility burned down on Boxing Day 2022 after someone put batteries in their red bin.

The fire meant the ACT had to truck around 50,000 tonnes of recyclables interstate for processing each year, at a cost of about $10 million annually. It also delayed the construction of Canberra’s Food Organics and Garden Organics (FOGO) facility (now expected to open in 2030).

Veolia CEO Craig Barker said delivering the $26 million facility would bring huge benefits to the Territory.

“This facility is where the ACT’s circular economy stops being an abstract policy goal and becomes everyday operational reality,” he said.

“When you look at a facility at this scale, the potential to process up to 115,000 tons here locally and, combined with our solar solution, we estimate around 26,000 tons of carbon will be avoided every year.”

Manteena and Veolia will work together to build the facility, with Veolia then running the MRF for the next 20 years.

Fire damaged or destroyed about 80 per cent of the Hume recycling facility on Boxing Day 2022. Photo: ACTFR.

The technology doesn’t exist yet to detect batteries earlier, but precautions will be taken to reduce the risk of another facility fire.

“When it comes to fire detection and suppression system … what we’re installing is significantly above the Australian standard,” Mr Barker said.

“[Technology for battery detection doesn’t exist] to the degree that we would like … but what we have is we have the ability in our contract, over 20 years, to innovate.

“So we will assess technology as and when it arrives to make sure that we can protect this facility.”

Both the ACT and Commonwealth governments have contributed $10.5 million each to the new MRF, and $5 million in insurance money will also be used.

The facility will feature high-speed optical-sorted, automated screens, and magnets to extract as many recyclables as possible.

A nation-leading feature will be the glass purification capability.

“[This] will allow us to crush and wash glass so that it can be used in re-manufacturing of glass products,” Mr Barker said.

“There’s not a lot of MRFs in Australia that would be able to wash and crush glass to colour grade.”

The old Hume Materials Recovery Facility has been demolished. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne said the glass washing capability would be a “game changer” for the Territory.

“Having a much higher quality glass product – [which] is highly sought after worldwide – we think this is something that we’ll be able to really be nation-leading on, and it will contribute overall to keeping costs down on this project,” she said.

“It’s going to be a world-class, state-of-the-art facility, one that has local jobs, brings recycling and materials recovery back to the ACT.”

The old facility could process about 60,000 tonnes of materials each year. The new hub will be able to recover almost double that amount.

Another aspect of the new facility will be the ability to once again see what Canberrans are and aren’t recycling, information that will support a dedicated education space at the MRF.

Veolia will invest $28 million in education over the course of the contract.

“[This] will allow us to make sure that the inbound stream is as clean as we possibly can, and then we can make sure that we end up with a really pure product at the back end that’s able to be recycled,” Mr Barker said.

Recycling Road will also be upgraded to improve access, safety and traffic flow within the Hume Resource Recovery Estate during construction and beyond.

Construction of the facility has been delayed for several reasons, including environmental approvals, the insurance payout and the development application process.

The new MRF is expected to open in early 2028.

“Ultimately, we’ve worked as quickly as we can while also ensuring that we’re future-proofing and delivering the best possible outcome for the Territory, with as many safeguards as possible, notwithstanding that we can’t mitigate all the risk,” Ms Cheyne said.

“This is a momentous occasion, and it’s one that’s been almost four years in the making.”

australia.title: Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor
australia.snippet: Former New Zealand prime minister will focus on leadership, social cohesion and public health in new role The former New Zealand prime mi...
australia.content:
The former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern will lecture and mentor at the University of Sydney after moving to Australia earlier this year.

Ardern begins this month and her work will focus on empathetic leadership, social cohesion and civic trust. The University of Sydney said Ardern would be based in its school of public health, exploring ways to address global health challenges and focusing on equity, inclusion and wellbeing.

The former prime minister will host guest lectures and masterclasses and will engage in mentoring, but the university said it was not a full-time teaching role.

“I’m delighted to be joining the University of Sydney,” Ardern said in a statement. “I’ve found myself especially focused on the question of leadership since leaving office – and how we can better support and encourage the kind of leadership needed to tackle our many global challenges.”

The University of Sydney vice-chancellor, Mark Scott, said he had long admired the courage and humanity Ardern brought to public life.

“Dame Jacinda led New Zealand through events of profound consequence and her leadership demonstrated that empathy and resolve do not compete with one another; each can strengthen the other,” he said.

“For our students, the opportunity to learn from Dame Jacinda is exceptional. They will meet not only a former prime minister, but a thoughtful teacher with a great deal to share about public leadership and service.”

In an ABC Conversations interview in July, Ardern said she believed people were seeking empathetic leadership despite many world leaders embodying a “dominant style” of leadership.

“You see people voting for parties [that] are often on the fringes of the mainstream. When you dive into the research, the majority of those who are doing that are often not voting for the ideology – they’re just voting against the status quo because they don’t think it serves them any more.

“So I think all the signs actually point to people wanting something different than what they’re getting now.”

Ardern retired from politics in January 2023, after more than five years as prime minister and the leader of the Labour party. She led the country through the Christchurch terrorist attack, the Whakaari volcanic eruption and the Covid pandemic.

In 2017, aged 37, Ardern became the world’s youngest-serving female leader, later becoming the second world leader to give birth while in office.

Ardern has since held fellowships at Harvard University focused on public leadership and technology governance, and published her memoir, A Different Kind of Power, in 2025.

Ardern, her husband Clarke Gayford and daughter Neve moved to Sydney earlier this year, purchasing a property in Sydney’s northern beaches for $5.3m.

australia.title: Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns
australia.snippet: Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’ Get our daily political e...
australia.content:
Australians should prepare for more basic and important online services to go offline unexpectedly, the nation’s signals intelligence agency has warned, urging that “system security must be prioritised over system availability”.

The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) also says businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarm that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.

In its annual cyber threat report, ASD warns hostile foreign governments, criminals and hackers are using AI to gather intelligence, disrupt critical infrastructure and steal money, and that Australians should fight fire with fire.

“We need AI tools to help automate our defences to stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers,” the ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, said on Monday.

“Australia must accelerate the modernisation of its technology and cybersecurity foundations to protect the systems we rely on every day.”

The annual threat report, released on Tuesday, revealed that ASD had responded to 1,500 cybersecurity incidents in the 2025-26 year, an increase of 20% from the previous year. It also notified external entities – including businesses, governments and critical infrastructure – of more than 4,400 potential malicious cyber incidents, up 80% in a year. AI is expected to accelerate those dangers in future.

ASD said government and private networks in Australia experienced “persistent” breach attempts from state-based actors last year, and claimed such actors “in the Indo-Pacific” could be launching attacks to prepare for potential future conflicts – including “future intelligence collection or disruption activities”.

The agency said the increasing availability of AI was creating positive opportunities, but also allowing cybercriminals and state-based actors to find vulnerabilities and launch attacks faster and more effectively. ASD warned “all network owners are facing elevated threat levels”, saying cybersecurity was now a “core business risk and leadership responsibility” for all organisations, no longer only a technical concern.

The report said integrating AI tools into cybersecurity functions could help find potential weaknesses or suspicious behaviour, and improve responses.

“To strengthen our cyber defences, we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment,” Bradshaw said.

She has spoken previously about ASD having access to Anthropic’s Mythos model, the powerful AI tool which the frontier lab said it couldn’t release publicly because it could identify unknown flaws in IT systems. While the use of AI by malicious actors is on the rise, Australian government agencies believe having access to such frontier models and collaborating with leading AI labs is critical to bolstering cybersecurity.

“To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences while harnessing AI’s benefit,” the defence minister, Richard Marles, said on the report’s release.

Tony Burke, the minister for home affairs and cybersecurity, said the government was “positioning Australia to respond to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by emerging technologies”.

Bradshaw said “legacy technology”, such as outdated systems or devices that were no longer supported with new updates by their creators, were among the biggest risks and most attractive targets for hackers. ASD called for Australia to modernise technology and cybersecurity capabilities, and said all organisations must take stronger action to ward off new threats.

Last week, newly discovered vulnerabilities in PHP – a programming language that underpins most websites – triggered a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem.

ASD urged organisations to update their systems, seek help from ASD and report suspicious incidents.

Bradshaw and Marles said organisations should prioritise the security of their systems over keeping them online, which could mean more services are forced to go offline while they are secured.

“In a threat environment transformed by AI, collective action is our strongest defence,” Bradshaw said.

australia.title: Man found dead in Queensland flood waters as state hit by multiple storms and days-long deluge
australia.snippet: Many rivers and roads left flooded after torrential downpours across Queensland Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podc...
australia.content:
A man’s body has been found in flood waters following an unusual weather system that delivered multiple storms and a days-long deluge to parts of Australia.

Emergency services were called to a creek at Boompa on Queensland’s Fraser Coast shortly after 11am on Monday after reports a man had been found unresponsive.

The man was declared dead after being found in Smothering Creek on Boompa Road, Queensland police said.

An investigation into his death has begun, with police to prepare a report for the coroner.

Further south, six campers were rescued after becoming stranded by flood waters at a public campground in Leyburn in Queensland’s Southern Downs.

Queensland Fire and Rescue Swiftwater crews responded to the call for help at 7.45am on Monday.

They rescued three men aged 71, 47 and 26 and two women aged 68 and 26 without incident at about 11.15am.

There were no reports of physical injuries, Queensland police said in a statement.

Torrential downpours across Queensland between Thursday and Monday left many rivers and roads flooded across the state’s south and east.

There are warnings of more rain and flooding to come.

Flash flooding hit Laidley Creek and Glenore Grove in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, closing some roads, Queensland police said on Monday.

The highest recorded four-day totals were spread across the state, with Blackdown Tableland, near Rockhampton, recording 439.4mm to early Monday.

Lower Springbrook, near the Gold Coast, recorded 325.2mm, while Nambour, near the Sunshine Coast, copped 314.2mm.

Brooweena, inland of K’gari, received 299.6mm.

Meteorologist Angus Hines said the system behind the downpours was unusual.

“The widespread rain bands with heaps of cloud cover, much cooler temperatures, and then the storms in that situation are really driven by what’s going on in the higher parts of the atmosphere,” he said.

On Sunday evening, thunderstorms were briefly connected from southern Queensland to Bass Strait, as a swift-moving system passed towards Australia’s east coast.

The storm band raced over most states, propelled by strong winds in the upper atmosphere.

“But that steering wind sort of just tapered off through the night last night over [Queensland’s] Darling Downs,” Hines said.

Flood warnings are current for Warrill Creek and the Bremer River in the Lockyer Valley, the Macintyre and Moonie rivers in the south, and the Mary River near the Sunshine Coast.

Western Queensland also remains on alert, with warnings current for the Warrego River at Charleville, the Bulloo River in Quilpie, and the Barcoo River at Blackall.

The Bureau of Meteorology said Queensland’s weather was set to return to more typical spring conditions as the week continued.

Hot and humid days are expected to give way to more subdued afternoon showers and storms.

australia.title: Steggall and Ryan accuse Taylor of not ’reading the room’ with ’tone deaf’ Haines tribute speech – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Steggall calls for civility and respect Independen...
australia.content:
Taylor not ‘reading the room’ in Haines speech, Steggall says

Sarah Basford Canales

Warringah MP Zali Steggall says she’s personally disappointed by Angus Taylor’s speech paying tribute to Helen Haines this morning, where the opposition leader denied any connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence.

The independent MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said “there is a link between our words and actions”.

At a press conference shortly before question time, Steggall said:

I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn. To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, makes sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of Parliament. And the same goes to the words and the images and the editorials used in media, social media ... what ads we authorise at election time for a party.

These were all part of Phil [Haines]’s speech to us this morning, his words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate.

We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.

Key events

  • 7h ago

    What we learned today, Monday 26 October

  • 8h ago

    Ryan hits out at ‘tone deaf’ Taylor comments after Haines attack

  • 9h ago

    Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

    Tanya Plibersek is asked if public life is safe for women

    Question time begins

    Haines’s first words after alleged attack relayed to parliament

    NSW to open gun buyback program bookings from noon today

    Taylor disagrees with link between parliamentary debate and violence

    Alleged attack on Haines ‘unfathomable’, Angus Taylor says

    ‘Helen Haines is a fighter’: PM

    Albanese pays tribute to Helen Haines in parliament

    MPs to place orange cockatoo sign on Haines’ seat in parliament
